The following test will make sure that all sheets have the same number of rows (212 participants), and will give an error message if not. It uses a loop to rename the sheets and label them. I did not write this myself, but I understand it! I will get there, I am determined! The first section is creating a list of each sheet from all the ten different data files and giving them a basic name. The second chunk is a loop that runs through all ten sheets and pulls every name (except for Participant, because it's merging on that). The "unlist" makes the all into one bigger vector with all the names. Then, the unique pulls out duplicated names and dup_names is telling R to list any it finds. The third chunk creates a function that targets only duplicated names and gives them the label assigned in the sheets chunk. So, if there are two "Other" columns, this makes them into "Other_Race" and "Other_Gender." The last chunk is then applying this function to each sheet/dataset. 
```{r}
sheets <- list(
  basic = harbour_data_basic, gender = harbour_data_gender,
  race = harbour_data_race, motivations = harbour_data_motivations,
  transportation = harbour_data_transportation,
  drugsinjected = harbour_data_drugsinjected,
  inhaled7days = harbour_data_inhaled7days,
  druglifetime = harbour_data_druglifetime,
  harbourhelped = harbour_data_harbourhelped,
  improve = harbour_data_improve
)

all_names <- unlist(lapply(sheets, function(d) setdiff(names(d), "PARTICIPANT")))
dup_names <- unique(all_names[duplicated(all_names)])
dup_names

make_unique <- function(d, label) {
  hit <- names(d) %in% dup_names
  names(d)[hit] <- paste0(names(d)[hit], "_", label)
  d
}

harbour_data_basic          <- make_unique(harbour_data_basic, "basic")
harbour_data_gender         <- make_unique(harbour_data_gender, "gender")
harbour_data_race           <- make_unique(harbour_data_race, "race")
harbour_data_motivations    <- make_unique(harbour_data_motivations, "motivations")
harbour_data_transportation <- make_unique(harbour_data_transportation, "transportation")
harbour_data_drugsinjected  <- make_unique(harbour_data_drugsinjected, "drugsinjected")
harbour_data_inhaled7days   <- make_unique(harbour_data_inhaled7days, "inhaled7days")
harbour_data_druglifetime   <- make_unique(harbour_data_druglifetime, "druglifetime")
harbour_data_harbourhelped  <- make_unique(harbour_data_harbourhelped, "harbourhelped")
harbour_data_improve        <- make_unique(harbour_data_improve, "improve")
```

Again, this is another test to ensure that each column has the same number of rows and stops and errors if not. It's using a loop to go through all datasets, rather than doing this individually for each of the 10. It returns the row and column count for each one. Then, the second chunk removes duplicates (assuming each sheet has 212 rows as planned), and then the ! = 1 asks if something is not equal to 1. Basically, if the row count is all 212, there will be one unique row value, thus a length of 1. If they are unequal, the value will not equal 1 and will trigger the rror in the curly bracket that stops the script and lists the count of each sheet. 
```{r}
dims <- lapply(sheets, dim)
row_counts <- sapply(dims, function(d) d[1])

if (length(unique(row_counts)) != 1) {
  stop("Row counts differ: ",
       paste(names(row_counts), row_counts, sep = "=", collapse = ", "))
}
```

# Now, Let's do some exploratory data analyses (EDA) on my Harbour data.

Next, time to Harbour is a little more difficult. 
```{r}
table(harbourdatafinaltrimmed$Time_To_Harbour, useNA = "ifany")
```

Here is a big code chunk that AI wrote for me. Let's see what it does.... It starts by cleaning the raw data of time to Harbour, then groups them into six groups, including NA. Then, it creates the factor, removes the clean_raw column and brings up a table with the count for each new category.  
```{r}
harbourdatafinaltrimmedtest <- harbourdatafinaltrimmed %>%
  mutate(
  
    clean_raw = trimws(as.character(Time_To_Harbour)),
    
    Time_Category = case_when(
      # Group 1: 15 minutes or less (includes 0, ranges <= 15, and "Few")
      clean_raw %in% c(
        "0", "no time - live on same street (0)", "0 to 15",
        "1", "1 to 10", "1 to 15", "2", "3", "5", "5 to 10",
        "6", "6 to 8 min", "7", "8", "10", "10 to 15 min",
        "13", "15", "15 or less", "Few"
      ) ~ "15 mins or less",
      
      # Group 2: 16 to 30 minutes (includes ranges up to 30 and midpoints around 18-30)
      clean_raw %in% c(
        "1 to 25 min", "18", "20", "21", "25", "30", "5 to 30"
      ) ~ "16 to 30 mins",
      
      # Group 3: 31 to 60 minutes (includes ranges spanning up to 60 and "2 min or 1 hr")
      clean_raw %in% c(
        "10 to 60", "15 to 60", "30 to 60", "40", "45", 
        "5 to 60", "60", "2 min or 1 hr"
      ) ~ "31 to 60 mins",
      
      # Group 4: Over 60 minutes (includes >60 mins, "1 to 180", and "Hours")
      clean_raw %in% c(
        "65", "69", "120", "135", "1 to 180", 
        "240 or 540 (see note)", "Hours"
      ) ~ "Over 60 mins",
      
      # Group 5: Unspecified / Vague valid responses (15 rows total)
      clean_raw %in% c("Minutes", "Minuites", "minuites", "Depends") ~ "~5 mins",
      
      # Group 6: Non-response and missing values (28 rows total)
      clean_raw %in% c("NR", "NR (see note)") | is.na(clean_raw) ~ NA_character_,
      
      TRUE ~ "CHECK_ME"
    ),
    
    Time_Category = factor(
      Time_Category,
      levels = c(
        "15 mins or less",
        "16 to 30 mins",
        "31 to 60 mins",
        "Over 60 mins",
        "~5 mins"
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  select(-clean_raw) 

table(harbourdatafinaltrimmedtest$Time_Category, useNA = "ifany")

```

I definitely could not write that code on my own but I can somewhat understand it, at least. I decided to change the minutes type to "~5 mins" because I didn't want it to be lost or "unspecified" as AI suggested. 

Next, using supplies at The Harbour will be the same method as the frequency one. Lets see if I can write it myself. 

The harbourdatafinaltrimmedtest (I will change this name later) accidentally ended up overriding the df. This should fix it. I had to rerun the chunk above where I named it and delete the one that broke it and then it worked.

```{r}
  harbourdatafinaltrimmedtest$Supplies_Harbour,
  levels = c("N", "S", "A"),
  labels = c("Never", "Sometimes", "Always"),
  ordered = TRUE
)
```

```{r}

is.ordered(harbourdatafinaltrimmedtest$Supplies_Harbour)
```
